visuals.title: Quiz
visuals.text: Ten questions across week five: Marco reads five, and five more are on the cards. Answer along, then hear Marco's answers.

quiz.pause_at: Pause here if you want to think it through

questions.q: A fund puts in 400 and takes out 800 five years later. Roughly what is the IRR?
questions.explain: Doubling in five years compounds at about 15% a year. 20% is simple interest: compounded, it gives about 2.5x.
questions.explain_at: Doubling in five years is about fifteen percent

questions.q: Harbour is bought at 10x EBITDA of 100 and sold at 8x EBITDA of 150. How much did the fall in the multiple cost the fund?
questions.explain: Two turns on 150 of EBITDA is 300, against 500 from growth and 200 from debt paydown: a net gain of 400.
questions.explain_at: The multiple: two turns lower on one hundred and fifty, minus three hundred

questions.q: Harbour is worth 450, with 400 of senior loans and 200 of bonds. What do the bondholders get, and who is the fulcrum?
questions.explain: Senior lenders take their 400 first, leaving 50 for the bonds. The fulcrum is the most senior layer not paid in full: the bonds.
questions.explain_at: The fulcrum is the most senior layer that isn't paid in full

questions.q: Harbour's leverage is 7.5x against a 7x covenant, and it pays all its interest. Is it in default?

options.text: Yes, the breach is a default
Not unless the equity is worthless

questions.explain: A covenant breach is a default even with no missed payment, so the sponsor asks for a waiver or puts in an equity cure.
questions.explain_at: A covenant breach is a default, missed payment or not

questions.q: Why shouldn't you divide Fitness Park's reported €600m price by its €461m of network revenue?

options.text: It shows a cheap deal at 1.3x
It leaves out the franchised clubs
Gyms are valued on members instead

questions.explain: Network revenue includes the franchised clubs' sales, most of which belong to the franchisees. And the €600m is unconfirmed, possibly equity, possibly EV.
questions.explain_at: Network revenue includes the sales of the franchised clubs

questions.q: Kone pays €5bn in cash and about €15.2bn in shares, and takes on €9.2bn of net debt. Roughly what is the equity value?
questions.explain: The sellers get 5 + 15.2 = about €20bn for the equity. Add the €9.2bn of net debt for the €29.4bn enterprise value.
questions.explain_at: Add up what Kone pays the sellers

questions.q: In 2020, why did the Advent and Cinven consortium win thyssenkrupp's lift business ahead of Kone?

options.text: They paid far more than Kone

questions.explain: Kone's offer roughly matched the price, but it dropped out over the risk that competition authorities would block it.
questions.explain_at: then dropped out over the risk that competition authorities would block it

questions.q: Over five years: EBITDA 590, depreciation 50, interest 240, tax at 25%. How much tax?
questions.explain: Tax is on profit: 590 − 50 − 240 = 300, and 25% of that is 75. Taxing EBITDA gives about 148.

questions.q: Who usually pays more for a business, a private equity fund or a company?

options.text: The fund, as it borrows more
The fund, as it pays less tax

questions.explain: Debt changes who funds the price, not the value. A company can pay for synergies; a fund can still win on certainty.
questions.explain_at: Debt changes who funds the price, not what the business is worth

questions.q: The undisturbed price is €20, rumours take it to €24, and the offer is €25. What's the premium?
questions.explain: Measure against the undisturbed price: 25 ÷ 20 − 1 = 25%. Against €24, already lifted by the rumours, it's about 4%.
questions.explain_at: Round five, taking a deal apart
